name: Carlos Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Milking starts at five, so I'm in the parlour at quarter to, with the radio on and 320 cows to get through. It's a twenty-point parlour, so ten cows a side, and you get a rhythm going: wipe, strip, clusters on, next. After breakfast I'm feeding, bedding the cubicles and checking the fresh calvers, and the afternoon is more of the same until second milking at three. I like the cows, I really do, each one's got a temper of her own. What wears me out is the feet, honestly, standing on concrete for ten hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work for, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's Brookfield Dairy, owned by Helen Ashworth, who's sixty-three and still drives the feeder wagon herself. I've been there two years and I'm the junior, so the head herdsman, Paddy, still checks my work on the fresh cows. At home it's me and Nadia, she's a nurse on the children's ward, mostly nights, so we leave each other notes on the fridge. My brother and I own a little flat in town together that we rent out, and I've got a good bit saved, so we're not worried about money day to day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. The cows wear collars that tell the herd software when one's coming into heat, and sometimes I paste a feed sheet into a chatbot and ask it to explain the numbers in normal words. I don't trust it on anything to do with a sick cow. For that I ask Paddy, or the vet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. The parlour stays the parlour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was mostly people trying to sell farmers expensive boxes. At work we'd joke about it in the tea room. Online I'd share something sarcastic about it, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the real fight was never AI anyway. It's the milk price, which the processor sets and we just take, and it's whether Helen keeps going or sells up. If AI is a flop, those are the same worries they were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and finally do the insemination course Helen keeps offering me, so I'm not just the guy who puts clusters on. Nadia and I would start saving properly for a house deposit, maybe in the next year or two. That's the plan anyway, robots or no robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd still worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen's age. If Helen sells, it won't be a robot that takes my job, it'll be a bloke from a property company in a clean jacket. That's the real risk on a farm like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools any more than you do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, probably, for the boring stuff, like checking the feed numbers. But the collars already do what they need to do. I'm not going to ask a chatbot whether a cow looks sad.

S0.say: I'd say the hype was mostly people trying to sell farmers expensive boxes. We'd joke about it in the tea room, and I'd probably share something sarcastic online.
S0.think: I think the real fight was never AI but the milk price the processor sets and whether my boss keeps going or sells up. If AI is a flop, those are the same worries as before.
S0.do: Keeps working and signs up for the cattle insemination course his boss has offered. Starts saving properly with his partner for a house deposit over the next year or two.
S0.feel: Calm, like an ordinary working day.
S0.quote: If Helen sells, it won't be a robot that takes my job, it'll be a bloke from a property company in a clean jacket.
S0.fieldNote: He sees the processor and his boss's age as the real threats, and AI as a sales pitch. His joke about the man from the property company was pointed: land sales scare him more than machines. He uses AI tools in a careful, limited way and keeps animal health questions for people he trusts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's basically the Mortons' farm down the road already. They put four milking robots in two years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in dairy aren't the problem, it's who gets the benefit. If a farm brings in robots, the workers should be trained and kept on, not shown the gate. I'd say the union should be at the table for that, and I'd say it at the branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my parlour job goes, but a different job turns up. Someone still has to fetch the cows that won't walk to the robot, clean the units, fix the arm at two in the morning. I'd want to be that guy, and I think I could be, if someone shows me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Helen this winter if I could spend a few days at the Mortons' to see how the robots work day to day. Then I'd ask her to pay for the robot maker's training course, which I think is about a week. And I'd use the chatbot more to read the data the robots spit out, because that's going to be half the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the useful kind. Like when a cow's off her feed and you know to watch her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think you'd miss, if the parlour went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rhythm, and knowing the cows by their back ends. The robot doesn't know that 412 kicks with her left leg. I do, and I've got the bruise to prove it. Maybe it learns, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Nadia say when you talk about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says the hospital's the same, new machines every year, and the good people learn them and the rest moan. She's right. She usually is, it's annoying.

S1.say: I'd say robots in dairy aren't the problem, it's who gets the benefit. Workers should be trained and kept on, and the union should be at the table, which I'd say at the branch meeting.
S1.think: I think my parlour job goes but a different one appears, fetching cows, cleaning units and fixing the robot arm at night. I'd want to be that person, and I think I could be if someone shows me.
S1.do: Asks his boss this winter to let him spend a few days at a neighbouring robot dairy. Asks her to pay for the week-long robot training course and uses AI tools more to read the robots' data.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but in a watchful, useful way.
S1.quote: The robot doesn't know that 412 kicks with her left leg. I do, and I've got the bruise to prove it.
S1.fieldNote: He has watched robots arrive next door and treats this picture as already half real. His instinct is to follow proof, learning from the neighbour first, and to bring the union in to protect workers. The cow that kicks with her left leg was his way of saying what a machine might miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Helen could have robots in by next autumn. I couldn't have a new career by next autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an emergency and it needs to be treated like one. Emergency income for people who lose work, and the union pushing for every farm that automates to pay into a fund. I'd post that and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, dairy goes first, because the robots already exist and work. I'm the junior, so I'm the first one out, before Paddy. And if AI can do almost any job, Nadia's ward changes too, and that's what really scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house deposit plan and keep the money where I can reach it. I'd go to every union meeting and push for that fund. After it arrives, I'd sign on for whatever help there is and wait to see where work still needs people, because I don't think anyone would know for the first few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, Helen can buy a robot but I can't buy a new trade. Two years is enough time for the farm to change and not enough time for me to. That's the whole problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip to see my grandmother in Lyon, which we'd been planning for her ninetieth. That one would hurt. Then the second car, Nadia and I could share.

S2.say: I'd say this is an emergency and should be treated like one, with emergency income for people who lose work. The union should push for every farm that automates to pay into a fund, and I'd post that.
S2.think: I think dairy goes first because the robots already exist, and as the junior I'm out before the head herdsman. If AI can do almost any job, my partner's hospital ward changes too, and that scares me most.
S2.do: Shelves the house deposit plan and keeps savings easy to reach. Pushes at union meetings for a fund paid by automating farms, then signs on for help and waits to see where work still needs people.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with his stomach dropping as he says it.
S2.quote: Two years is enough time for the farm to change and not enough time for me to.
S2.fieldNote: His fear spread quickly from his own job to his partner's, which is what pushed him from uneasy to alarmed. His plan is collective and defensive, through the union and public help, with no career move he trusts. He noted that the farm can change faster than he can, which shaped everything he said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still quick. But I could at least get a trade under my belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to train people, now, not when it's already happened. Government and the robot companies should pay for courses while people still have jobs. I'd say it in the tea room and at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd become a robot technician, the guy in the van who fixes the milking robots. But I know that's only a bridge. If AI can do almost any job by 2031, then eventually it fixes its own robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the robot maker's course in the first year and apply to the dealer that services the farms round here. They're always short of people. I'd bank the extra money from that job, every bit of it above what I earn now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was doing something. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's only a bridge. Why cross it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a bridge is still better than standing in the river. Four years of good wages and learning how the machines think is worth something. And I'd meet every farmer in the area, which matters later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your plans with Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably hold off on kids for a bit, until we saw how it was going. We talked about trying in a couple of years. Five years of not knowing is a long time to wait, though.

S3.say: I'd say now is the time to train people, not after it's happened. The government and robot companies should pay for courses while people still have jobs, and I'd say that at work and at the union.
S3.think: I think I'd become a robot technician, the person in the van who fixes milking robots. I know it's only a bridge, because by 2031 AI may fix its own robots too.
S3.do: Takes the robot maker's course in the first year and applies to the local dealer that services farm robots. Banks every bit of extra pay above his current wage.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier for having a plan to act on.
S3.quote: Because a bridge is still better than standing in the river.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gave him a concrete move he believes in: robot servicing, which he has seen work for others. He was clear-eyed that it's temporary and chose it anyway, for the wages and the contacts. Having children came up for the first time here, as something he'd put off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Helen will have retired by then, one way or another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make sure ordinary people own a share of this, not just investors. Workers' co-ops, public money, the lot. I'd be saying that everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think about Helen's farm. Her kids don't want it. If a few of us workers formed a co-op and bought in over time, we could run it with robots and keep the money local. If the robots are going to milk the cows anyway, I want to own a bit of the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot course in the first year anyway, so I understand the kit. Then I'd sit down with Paddy and two lads from the Mortons' and talk about a co-op, and look at what our savings add up to. I'd put my share of the flat money aside for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than the others. Ten years feels like a plan instead of a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change, compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five, I'm grabbing a bridge. With ten, I can build the bridge and charge a toll. Sorry, that sounds greedy, but you know what I mean, it's about owning instead of being owned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Helen when you raised the co-op idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you built this, and we'd like it to stay a working farm with your name on the gate. She'd probably laugh at me first. Then she'd ask to see the numbers, because that's Helen.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to make sure ordinary people own a share of this, not just investors. I'd push for workers' co-ops and public money everywhere I could.
S4.think: I think a few workers could form a co-op and buy into my boss's farm over time, since her children don't want it. If robots will milk the cows anyway, I want to own part of the robot.
S4.do: Takes the robot course in the first year to understand the equipment. Meets colleagues to plan a workers' co-op, works out their combined savings and sets aside his share of the flat income for it.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful, as if he has a plan instead of a fire.
S4.quote: With ten, I can build the bridge and charge a toll.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turned his union politics into ownership: a co-op of workers buying into the farm. He was a little embarrassed by how business-like it sounded, but the idea was detailed and clearly not new. His caution remained, since he'd still take the robot course first to understand the kit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The robots are already in the shed next door, so for dairy that one isn't science fiction. What would help is the union having real power when farms automate, and income support that's there on day one, not after six months of forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask what happens to the villages. Our pub's only open four nights a week as it is. If the farms don't need people, I don't know who's left to drink in it.

headlineQuote: If the robots are going to milk the cows anyway, I want to own a bit of the robot.
portrait: Carlos Dubois is a 27-year-old junior herdsman on a 320-cow dairy, with a nurse partner, solid savings and half a rented-out flat with his brother. He uses AI tools now and then for paperwork but trusts people with sick cows, and he has watched a neighbouring farm switch to milking robots. A union member, he believes the question is who benefits from automation, not whether it happens. In AI Plateau and Steady Disruption he plans to learn the robots, while AGI by 2028 alarms him because it moves faster than he can retrain. With five years he would become a robot technician as a bridge, and with ten he would try to form a workers' co-op to buy into his boss's farm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because milking robots already exist and his farm could switch faster than he could learn a new trade.
whatWouldHelp: Unions with real power when farms automate, and income support that starts on day one instead of after months of forms.
